howWeWork.heading: How we work
howWeWork._comment: Register is deliberately calibrated: we propose, the client approves — design ownership stays with the client, explicitly. Stages 3 and 4 carry emphasis: 3 answers the repeatability question, 4 (short runs → full series) is the most underused advantage vs Asian suppliers.

steps.title: Drawing review
steps.body: Send a drawing, a 3D file or a physical sample. We come back with a manufacturability assessment: where a detail drives cost, where a radius or a joint can be simplified without changing the design intent, and what it means for tooling. You decide what to change.

steps.title: Sampling
steps.body: A first physical sample from the actual process that will run in series — not a hand-made one-off. What you approve is what production repeats.

steps.title: Tooling and fixtures
steps.body: Punching dies, jigs and welding fixtures are designed and built in-house to the part. This is why the second thousand looks like the first.

steps.title: Series production
steps.body: Short runs and full series on the same equipment. A model can launch as a market test and scale to full volume without changing supplier or re-tooling.

steps.title: Finishing
steps.body: Powder coating for metal, spray painting for MDF and panels — both lines in-house. Finishing is not subcontracted, so colour and adhesion stay inside one quality chain.

steps.title: Packing and dispatch
steps.body: Packed to your specification, labelled under your brand, ready for your warehouse or direct dispatch.

repeatability.heading: The same part, batch after batch
lines: Two Fanuc welding robots and a Kuka sanding robot run in the metal chain.
Dies, jigs and welding fixtures are built in-house to the part — geometry does not drift between batches.
